description: 🚀 We are a family team exploring space, science, and technology together. Our child leads the ideas, while his parents provide support. We welcome other kids who love space, science, coding, design, or creative ideas. No advanced skills needed—just curiosity and enthusiasm! Let’s learn and build together! 🌎
summary: Satellite maps are silent. Typhoon Jukebox gives a typhoon a sound. Choose any named storm of the 2026 Pacific typhoon season — or build a typhoon of your own — and hear its whole life, from formation to dissipation, as a short symphony: wind speed sets the pitch, air pressure sets the weight of the bass, and every landfall lands as a single strike scaled by its strength. All of the music is synthesized in real time from the storm's real record — no samples, no recordings. On screen, the storm's track crosses a real satellite map while nine hand-drawn strength symbols, drawn by our 9-year-old team leader, show how strong it is at every moment. Designed by a 9-year-old typhoon fan, for typhoon enthusiasts everywhere.
details:
Typhoon Jukebox is a web app that lets you listen to a typhoon's whole life. On the entry screen you choose: replay a real typhoon (the named storms of 2026, listed by month) or create your own typhoon (pick its peak strength, name it, choose the month it forms, and generate its life). In the player, the storm's track is drawn across a real satellite map, and the team leader's hand-drawn strength symbol — one of nine — moves along the track, showing how strong the storm is at every moment; beside the map, the storm's cloud imagery is shown from NASA Worldview. A gramophone plays the storm's music while a wind-speed curve traces its rise and fall through five chapters — Formation, Growth, Peak, Weakening, Dissipation — and a narration line tells the storm's story as it plays.

How the sound works. One rule set, used for every storm: wind speed sets the pitch — lead strings climb the A-minor scale as the wind rises, their long notes overlapping with a reverb tail, over a string pad cycling Am–F–C–G. Air pressure sets the weight of the bass — the double bass, contrabassoon and tuba are fed the current pressure, so the bigger the pressure drop, the lower and heavier they sound. The rate of intensification sets the density — a timpani and low-string pulse quickens from 0.48 seconds to 0.19 seconds as the storm strengthens, and the faster a storm intensifies, the denser its notes. French horns join at Category 3, the full brass at Category 4, and a brass chord slams down at the peak. Wind is string tremolo and breathy flute, flowing continuously; rain is pizzicato, celesta and harp raindrops that thicken with intensity; thunder is timpani rolls and low brass. A landfall is a single strike — low timpani with a soft cymbal brush — whose loudness is scaled by the wind speed at the moment of landfall: Bavi's first landfall, on Rota Island at its 155 kt peak after the hush of the eye passing, is the heaviest hit in the piece, while its second landfall, on the Zhejiang coast at about 70 kt, is audibly smaller. As a storm weakens, the pitch falls, the rhythm thins and the sound fades with its remnant circulation. Everything is synthesized in real time from the data — no samples are used.

About the data. The library holds every named storm of the 2026 Pacific typhoon season — 32 storms, from Nokaen in January to Cempaka in November. Storm records are compiled from Wikipedia's "2026 Pacific typhoon season" (JMA naming and peak-intensity records, JTWC categories; checked 11 November 2026). Each storm's playback curve is a sonified interpretation generated from its real peak intensity and lifespan — Bavi's curve, including its eyewall-replacement dip and its two landfalls, is anchored to its JTWC best-track positions — and the pressure shown during playback is an estimate derived from wind speed. The track maps use Esri World Imagery satellite tiles as their base, and every storm's player links to NASA Worldview, where the storm's real VIIRS true-color cloud imagery can be viewed. This page turns typhoon data into sound as a demonstration; it is not an official warning. For evacuation and official guidance, always follow your local meteorological agency.

Built as a web application (HTML/JavaScript, Web Audio API). The nine hand-drawn strength symbols were drawn by the 9-year-old team leader, who also collected the data and designed the number-to-sound mapping; the user interface was proposed by his mother and decided by him; the website was built by his father.

Disclaimer: This is not an official warning system. For evacuation and safety information, always follow the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).

AI Use Declaration: AI assistants were used by the team: the 9-year-old team leader worked together with AI on data collection, the number-to-sound mapping design, and building the website, under parental supervision. The nine strength symbols are his own hand drawings. All narration in submitted materials is text-to-speech (a synthetic voice) — the child's real voice and image are not used in any submitted material, for privacy.
dataRefs: NASA Worldview — VIIRS true-color satellite imagery. Every storm in the library links from its player to that storm's real cloud imagery in NASA Worldview (\"Open this day in NASA Worldview\").
projectRefs: Wikipedia, \"2026 Pacific typhoon season\" — storm names, dates, peak-intensity and category records compiled from JMA and JTWC reports; the source of the library's storm records (checked 11 November 2026).
